title: Taliban Energy Deal: From Delta Investment To Regional Competition
gist: Saudi private firm Delta has signed a $200 million oil and gas exploration contract with the Taliban's Ministry of Mines & Petroleum for Kushk-Tirpul in western Afghanistan, wrapped in talk of a ~$50 billion, 25-year programme and a ~700km, ~$10 billion pipeline to the Pakistani border. The USGS resource base is tiny, nothing is proven or financed, and the revival of the 1990s CentGas name plus Zalmay Khalilzad's presence gives the deal a geopolitical read that the underlying geology and financing do not yet support.

insights.claim: The Taliban's Ministry of Mines & Petroleum has valued the Kushk-Tirpul exploration contract with Saudi company Delta at $200 million, the only committed number in the deal.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: The real signed exposure is two orders of magnitude below the headline; price the deal off $200 million, not $50 billion.
insights.locator: The Taliban’s Ministry of Mines & Petroleum has valued

insights.claim: Delta describes an integrated programme with potential investment capacity of up to around $50 billion over 25 years, but that figure is neither guaranteed nor pre-financed.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Treat the $50 billion as marketing optionality; the gap between announced and financed capex is the whole trade.
insights.quote: That figure does not represent guaranteed or pre-financed investment.
insights.locator: However, the programme presented by Delta

insights.claim: The $200 million contract, the proposed $10 billion pipeline and the potential $50 billion programme are three different tiers of a long-term plan and should not be presented as a single financial commitment.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for frontier resource announcements: separate signed contract, conditional infrastructure and aspirational programme.
insights.quote: are therefore three different levels of a long-term plan and should not be presented as a single financial commitment
insights.locator: The $200 million contract, the proposed $10 billion pipeline

insights.claim: The proposed roughly 700-kilometre pipeline from near Guzara in Herat to the vicinity of Spin Boldak in Kandahar, branded 'CentGas - Corridor of Prosperity', has been costed at around $10 billion but remains at study stage with construction not approved.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: No FID, no permits, no financing: the pipeline is an option, not a contracting opportunity for EPC or steel demand yet.
insights.locator: The third component is a proposed roughly 700-kilometre pipeline

insights.claim: The Kushk-Tirpul project area covers about 23,317 square kilometres, with planned geological and geophysical studies, seismic surveys, exploratory drilling and reservoir assessment.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Defines a multi-year exploration timeline before any production decision, so near-term cash flows are zero.
insights.locator: According to information released by Delta

insights.claim: A 2009 US Geological Survey assessment put mean undiscovered resources in Tirpul at roughly 21.55 million barrels of oil, 44.76 billion cubic feet of natural gas and about 0.91 million barrels of natural gas liquids - volumes far too small to underwrite a multibillion-dollar pipeline.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: The only independent subsurface estimate available is an order of magnitude short of corridor-scale economics; the burden of proof sits on the drill bit.
insights.quote: mean undiscovered resources in Tirpul at around 21.55 million barrels of oil, 44.76 billion cubic feet of natural gas and about 0.91 million barrels of natural gas liquids
insights.locator: Kushk–Tirpul: Geological Potential, Not Proven Reserves

insights.claim: The USGS figure of about 8,700 square kilometres refers only to the area the 2009 study examined and should not be confused with the much larger area covered by the new Kushk-Tirpul contract.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Guards against acreage-based extrapolation that would inflate the implied resource estimate.
insights.locator: That figure refers to the area examined

insights.claim: Previous studies recorded oil indications including leakage from an abandoned well in Tirpul, but no significant commercial production has ever been reported from the basin, and earlier seismic collection in Kushk faced security, technical and operational difficulties.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Historical failure to convert shows into production is the base rate that should anchor expectations for Delta.
insights.locator: Previous studies recorded indications of oil

insights.claim: Delta's first real test is proving reserves large enough to justify further major investment, which requires exploratory drilling to establish how much is technically and economically recoverable.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Drilling results, not signing ceremonies, are the first genuine catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: Delta’s first real test, therefore

themes.theme: Sequencing: Herat first, regional corridor later

insights.claim: Delta's programme has three components in sequence: exploration and possible production at Kushk-Tirpul, a study of supplying gas to Herat city, its industrial park and power generation, and only then the Guzara-Spin Boldak pipeline.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Each phase gates the next, so slippage compounds; the realistic near-term deliverable is a Herat domestic gas study.
insights.locator: Delta’s announced programme has three main components.

insights.claim: If usable resources are found, Herat's domestic market - city, industrial park and power generation - would become the first consumer, not export markets.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Domestic gas-to-power in Herat is the low-capex path and the earliest observable proof of concept.
insights.locator: The second is a study of how gas could be used in Herat.

insights.claim: A pipeline of this scale requires a sufficiently large gas consumption or export market, which pulls Pakistan and wider South Asian markets directly into the project's economics.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Offtake, not geology alone, determines whether this becomes a regional corridor; track any Pakistani purchase commitment.
insights.locator: Such a pipeline would also require a sufficiently large market

themes.theme: CentGas redux and the Khalilzad question

insights.claim: The 1997 CentGas consortium to move Turkmen gas through Afghanistan to Pakistan was led by US company Unocal with a 46.5 per cent stake, with Saudi firm Delta Oil holding 15 per cent as one of its main partners.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Establishes that today's Saudi counterparty is the same name that failed at this once before, in easier conditions.
insights.locator: In 1997, a consortium called CentGas was formed

insights.claim: The original trans-Afghan gas corridor was always geopolitical: it could have reduced the region's dependence on Russian transit networks while keeping Iran out of a potential gas route to South Asia.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: The same two exclusions define the strategic value today, which is why non-commercial sponsorship may keep the project alive past commercial logic.
insights.quote: It could have reduced the region’s dependence on Russian transit networks while keeping Iran out of a potential gas route to South Asia.
insights.locator: From the outset, CentGas was not merely an economic project.

insights.claim: Afghanistan's political and security conditions killed the original project, Unocal withdrew from the consortium in 1998, and the trans-Afghan concept survived only as the TAPI pipeline.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: A 28-year track record of non-delivery is the relevant prior for any trans-Afghan pipeline headline.
insights.locator: However, Afghanistan’s political and security conditions

insights.claim: Zalmay Khalilzad, who worked on political-risk issues for Unocal's Afghan projects in the 1990s via Cambridge Energy Research Associates, attended the Kabul signing ceremony and earlier meetings with Taliban officials alongside Delta's chief executive.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Continuity of dealmakers across three decades is the strongest signal that this is a revived political project, not a new commercial one.
insights.locator: Zalmay Khalilzad provides another link

insights.claim: No credible public document identifies Khalilzad as a shareholder, director or employee of Delta, and the US State Department says he is not a US government employee and acts entirely in a personal capacity.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Do not price implicit US government backing into the deal; there is no official sponsor behind the ceremony optics.
insights.quote: Zalmay Khalilzad is not an employee of the United States government. Therefore, he does not represent the US government and conducts all of his activities in a personal capacity.
insights.locator: The US State Department told Afghanistan International

insights.claim: Khalilzad's repeated presence raises questions about a private or advisory role but should not be read as evidence of US government support for the project.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Separates personal dealmaking from state policy, which matters for sanctions and political-risk assumptions.
insights.locator: Jennifer Murtazashvili, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh

insights.claim: A private Saudi company signing a contract does not mean the Saudi government or its sovereign funds have committed $50 billion to Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Blocks the common misread that this is Riyadh state capital entering Afghanistan; check for sovereign co-investment before assuming it.
insights.quote: Delta is also a private Saudi company, and there is still no indication of direct Saudi government involvement in the project.
insights.locator: Delta is also a private Saudi company

themes.theme: TAPI linkage is optionality, not agreement

insights.claim: Before the new agreement, Delta proposed participating in TAPI with long-term purchases of Turkmen gas, investment to raise capacity at the Galkynysh field, and a Guzara-to-Spin Boldak pipeline, potentially extended under a separate Pakistani agreement toward the Indian border and Gwadar port.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Reveals Delta's real ambition is a regional gas trading position, which would compete with or absorb TAPI volumes.
insights.locator: According to remarks by Abdul Ghani Baradar

insights.claim: There is no announced agreement formally linking the new pipeline to TAPI or committing Pakistan to buy or transport the gas, so the connection is a strategic possibility rather than a confirmed element.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Headlines merging the Delta deal with TAPI are ahead of the documentation; require a Pakistani offtake agreement as confirmation.
insights.quote: the connection between the two projects is a strategic possibility rather than a confirmed element of the agreement
insights.locator: How Is the New ‘CentGas’ Connected to TAPI?

insights.claim: TAPI and the Delta programme have opposite logics: under TAPI Turkmenistan supplies the gas and Afghanistan is transit, while Delta's first objective is to discover Afghan resources and use some domestically.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: If Delta succeeds, Afghanistan shifts from transit country to producer, changing the regional gas map and Turkmen leverage.
insights.locator: Under TAPI, the main source of gas is Turkmenistan

insights.claim: The Taliban ministry issued a 2023 request for expressions of interest promising an open, transparent and competitive award for Kushk and Tirpul, but the qualified-company list, assessment results and documents explaining Delta's selection are not easily accessible in its public archive.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Opaque award processes raise later challenge risk and complicate due diligence for any bank or partner joining the project.
insights.locator: How Was the Contract Awarded to Delta?

insights.claim: China's experience shows signing a contract in Afghanistan does not guarantee implementation: Mes Aynak copper and Amu Darya oil both faced delays and disputes, and in 2025 the Taliban cancelled a 25-year Amu Darya oil contract with a Chinese company for failing to meet commitments.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: The most recent comparable, backed by far deeper Chinese pockets, was terminated - a direct base rate for Delta's 25-year deal.
insights.locator: China’s investment experience in Afghanistan also shows

insights.claim: Very limited international recognition of the Taliban government and sanctions on several Taliban leaders create legal and political risk for banks, insurers and international companies, even though they do not make foreign investment impossible.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Financing and insurance, not geology, are the likely binding constraint on any multibillion-dollar phase.
insights.locator: The Challenge of Legitimacy and Contract Durability

insights.claim: A future Afghan government is expected to review the Delta agreement and similar Taliban-signed contracts to judge whether they benefited the Afghan people, which is itself a commercial risk for a 25-year investment.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Contract durability risk should be priced into any 25-year Afghan resource exposure alongside geology and security.
insights.quote: I very strongly question whether a ruling group that lacks legitimacy should be allowed to sell the natural resources of the Afghan nation.
insights.locator: Annie Pforzheimer, a former deputy chief of mission

insights.claim: Actual exploration or production under the Delta agreement may still be years away, with the deal mainly indicating that a Saudi company wants a future role in Afghanistan's energy market.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year horizon before any physical output, so treat this as positioning rather than supply.
insights.locator: Annie Pforzheimer, a former deputy chief of mission

insights.claim: Routing the pipeline to Spin Boldak makes Pakistan indispensable for turning a domestic Afghan line into a regional corridor, at a moment when Taliban-Pakistan relations are strained over the TTP and wider security disputes.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Afghan-Pakistani security friction is the key non-geological gate on the corridor thesis; watch TTP-related escalation as a project indicator.
insights.locator: Pakistan and Iran: Two Regional Variables

insights.claim: Saudi investment could create some space for mediation between the Taliban and Pakistan, but fundamental security disputes will not be resolved by an economic project alone.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Limits the diplomatic upside case; do not assume pipeline economics can buy a Kabul-Islamabad settlement.
insights.locator: Murtazashvili believes the presence of Saudi investment

insights.claim: Herat's extensive trade, fuel, electricity and transit links with Iran mean any domestic Afghan gas supply to western Afghanistan would gradually erode Tehran's economic influence there.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: Import substitution in Herat is a slow-burn negative for Iranian fuel and power exports and a potential source of friction.
insights.locator: Iran may also follow the project closely.

insights.claim: Geopolitical competition between Iran and Gulf actors over Afghan transit and energy markets could emerge if Saudi investment expands, but it is premature to call it now given the Taliban's active relations with Tehran and Iran's role as a major economic partner.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: A contingent, not current, rivalry: escalate the theme only if Delta moves past exploration.
insights.locator: It is therefore premature to speak of definite Iran-Saudi competition

insights.claim: The project's fate will be decided by initial survey and drilling results, Delta's ability to attract financing and technical partners, the existence of a gas market and the durability of the political framework - not by the $50 billion headline.
insights.speaker: Reza Farzam
insights.so_what: A four-part checklist for judging progress; signing a contract is explicitly the easiest stage.
insights.quote: signing a contract is the easiest stage of such a project
insights.locator: From a $200 Million Contract to a $50 Billion Dream
